title: machine_report.v1
description: Machine-readable report of one yandex-tank run (report.json). Written once by the MachineReport plugin in post_process and never modified afterwards; everything computed later lives in separate files next to it. Units are part of field names: *_ts is unix time in seconds (UTC), *_s seconds, *_ms milliseconds, *_us microseconds, *_rps requests per second, *_instances generator instances, *_cores CPU cores, *_pct percent (0..100); objects with a unit field (monitoring metrics, saturation signals) carry the unit there. Time windows are half-open: [start_ts, end_ts). Objects are open: consumers MUST ignore unknown fields. Within v1 an optional field may be added; a new enum value may be written only after the CLI that knows it is released, because an older CLI rejects the report. Removing, renaming or changing the type or meaning of a field requires machine_report.v2.

config_sha256.description: Informational, not a comparability key (that is load_profile_sha256): the effective config also holds run-specific values (metaconf labels, the microscope of the plugin section, local ammo paths), so runs of one config usually differ here. sha256 of the effective tank config serialized as json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':'), ensure_ascii=False) after masking: a value is replaced with *** for a key, a header string 'Name: value' (also in square brackets, as in pandora and phantom headers) or a URL query parameter whose name, case-insensitively, is authorization or cookie or contains token, secret, password, passwd, oauth, ticket or key. Masking goes by name only: it keeps the hash stable when a token rotates and does not guarantee that no secret is left.

load_profile_sha256.description: sha256 of provenance.load_profile serialized as canonical JSON (RFC 8785): keys sorted, no whitespace, UTF-8. load_profile holds only integers, null and profileString strings, so this is exactly json.dumps(load_profile, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')) in Python and encoding/json of the decoded map in Go; report.Validate recomputes it. Runs with different values are not comparable.

load_profile.description: Normalized load profile: everything that decides how the target is loaded and nothing run-specific (local paths, URLs, timestamps, hosts). Closed: a new field would change the hash of every later run, so any change of this object needs machine_report.v2.

pools.description: One entry per generator pool in config order: pandora pools, phantom multi sections; a single-pool config has one entry.

gun.description: Gun of the pool as configured: the pandora gun type (http, http2, grpc, connect or a custom gun name), phantom or bfg. A jmeter run gets no report: a jmx plan is not expressible as load_type and schedule.

transport.description: http1: HTTP/1.1 without TLS; http1_tls: HTTP/1.1 over TLS; h2: HTTP/2 over TLS; h2c: HTTP/2 without TLS; other.

target_protocol.description: What the target speaks on top of the transport. grpc also when gRPC is shot by an HTTP/2 gun over h2c: an HTTP/2 pool over h2c is grpc unless the plugin section overrides target_protocol of the pool to http, because a gRPC target taken for HTTP would get its error share from HTTP 200 and look clean.

load_type.description: What the schedule sets: rps, or busy instances (stepper load_type instances). stpd_file: a prepared stpd file, which holds both the schedule and the requests; then schedule is empty and ammo_sha256 is the sha256 of the stpd bytes.

schedule.description: Schedule steps in config order, normalized: whitespace removed, numbers in the shortest decimal form without exponent and trailing zeros, durations in seconds with suffix s (const(10,1m) becomes const(10,60s), 3h2m3s becomes 10923s, 0.3s stays 0.3s); pandora schedule entries are written in the same form, e.g. line(1,10,300s).

startup.description: Instances startup schedule of pandora, same normalization; empty when not set. Empty for phantom and bfg: they start all instances at once, and their instances schedule is schedule with load_type instances.

instances.description: Instances limit of the generator pool: pandora the instances its startup schedule starts, phantom and bfg the instances they shoot with (the instances option for rps, the total of the schedule for instances; times green_threads_per_instance for the green bfg worker); null when not set.

ammo_type.description: Ammo format as configured (uri, phantom, http/json, grpc/json, ...); null when the gun builds requests itself.

ammo_sha256.description: sha256 of the ammo of the pool, not of its path or URL. An ammo file: sha256 of the bytes the gun read (after download and decompression); for pandora, the local file of each pool from the patched pandora config (pandora_config_*.yaml). Inline ammo written in the config (pandora ammo.uris, phantom and bfg uris): sha256 of the UTF-8 bytes of json.dumps(<the list as configured>, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':'), ensure_ascii=False). null when the pool reads no ammo file and no inline ammo (the gun builds requests itself or takes them from a provider the plugin does not know); such pools differ in load_profile_sha256 only by the rest of the pool.

labels.description: Run labels as passed in metaconf.firestarter.labels; {} when the config has none.

series.description: Copy of labels.series; null when the run belongs to no series.

test_id.description: Load Testing test id when the tank knows it, otherwise null. The tank config does not carry it (ulta does not pass it), so the plugin writes null, and a consumer takes the id from where it fetched the files.

tank_job_id.description: core.test_id of the effective tank config.

run_id.description: Id of the execution that launched the tank (tank plant, CI), when known.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 time the report was written.

statuses.description: What the plugin can know when it writes the report: how the shooting ended and whether the requested data was collected. Suitability, the analysis verdict and the AI status are computed later and live in analysis.json and verdict.json.

autostop_criterion.description: Autostop criterion that stopped the run, as written in the config; null unless status is AUTOSTOPPED.

completeness.description: COMPLETE: every requested source is ok. PARTIAL: some source is not ok, but no required source is empty, error or unsupported. INCOMPLETE: a required source is empty, error or unsupported; then blocking is true and the completeness check turns the flow red.

blocking_sources.description: Ids of required monitoring sources that made the report INCOMPLETE.

phases.description: Planned load profile, one entry per schedule step of every pool; offsets count from the schedule start, which is start_ts of the test window. from_rps and to_rps are set for load_type rps, from_instances and to_instances for load_type instances, both of the pool of the phase. Indexes are unique and run through all pools. A phase has started when test.start_ts + start_offset_s < test.end_ts, and a started phase has its phase-<index> window.

pool.description: Index of the pool in provenance.load_profile.pools whose schedule step this is; the plugin writes it for every phase, and report.Validate checks that it names a pool.

windows.description: Aggregates over time windows: the whole shooting (id test), every started phase (id phase-<index>) and, for const phases, the phase without its first and last trim seconds when at least a second is left (id steady-<index>; trim from the plugin section, default 15 s). A second is the second a response was received in, int(send_ts + interval_real / 1e6), as in the tank aggregator; load.per_second and hist.v1 use the same seconds. The test window is [S, E): E is the last second with data plus one; S, the schedule start, is the first second with data minus the zero-plan steps that open the schedule (the smallest total over pools, e.g. const(0,10s)). A phase window is [S + floor(start_offset_s), max(its start + 1, min(E, S + ceil(start_offset_s + duration_s)))), so a once phase and a phase started less than a second before E get a one-second window, where 0 responses are allowed. A steady window is [S + ceil(start_offset_s) + trim, min(E, S + floor(start_offset_s + duration_s)) - trim). Responses that arrive after the load stopped belong to the test window; a phase whose start falls only into that tail counts as started and gets a short window. With several pools a phase and steady window follows the step of its own pool, while responses, codes, latency, monitoring and CPU in it are of the whole shooting. Latency, codes, monitoring and generator and target CPU are all given per window, so every consumer computes from the same windows. The test window and every steady window have an entry in generator.cpu.windows (unless its source is unavailable), in target.cpu.windows (unless target.cpu is null) and in every metric of an ok or partial monitoring source. JSON Schema cannot say this; report.Validate checks it, as well as unique ids, every window being within the test window and at least a second long, the number in phase-<n> and steady-<n> being equal to phase_index, a phase-<n> window for every started phase, phase_index of a window naming a phase of phases, a steady window only for a const phase, responses equal to net codes without 777, and the quantile rank rule of $defs/latencyMs. Integers are read by value: 240.0 and 2.4e2 are 240, as in JSON Schema.

version.description: Generator version: pandora from `pandora -version` (the pandorax build from `Pandora X - <version>`, else `Pandora core/<version>`); null when the gun has no source yet (phantom, bfg). Informational in comparisons until the calibration (T11).

grpc_status.description: How the gRPC status of a response reaches this report. grpc_codes: raw statuses in grpc_codes. http_mapped: the gun maps statuses to HTTP-like codes in http_codes (pandora grpc gun: OK to 200, Unavailable to 503, several statuses to 400), errors are visible but lossy. not_read: the target speaks gRPC, but the gun does not read grpc-status (h2c gun without trailers, LOAD-3823, also an HTTP/2 pool over h2c without the target_protocol override), so a gRPC error with HTTP 200 is invisible and the error share is unknown. not_applicable: no pool speaks gRPC. With several gRPC pools the weakest wins: not_read over http_mapped over grpc_codes, while code_kinds still lists grpc if some pool reports raw statuses. So grpc_codes requires grpc in code_kinds, http_mapped and not_read require http, and grpc in code_kinds requires a gRPC pool.

gun.description: Generator of the run; transport and target protocol of every pool are in provenance.load_profile.

code_kinds.description: Which code maps the generator provides; windows and per_second carry exactly these maps. net is always present. http when responses carry an HTTP status; the pandora grpc gun reports http too: it maps gRPC statuses to HTTP-like codes (OK to 200, Unavailable to 503, several statuses to 400), so the mapping is lossy. grpc only when the generator reports raw gRPC statuses of at least one pool (h2c with grpc-status read from trailers, LOAD-3823). A kind missing here means the generator does not provide it, not that there were no such codes.

autostop_criteria.description: Autostop criteria as written in the config, in order, e.g. quantile(99,500ms,10s); empty when autostop is off. The analysis needs every configured threshold, not only the one that fired.

per_second.description: One entry per second of the test window [start_ts, end_ts), ascending and without holes; report.Validate checks it. The tank aggregator does not deliver a second without responses, and the plugin adds it: rps 0, empty code maps, planned_rps from the schedule, instances null.

artifacts.description: Files written next to report.json; paths are relative to it.

histograms.description: Per-second latency histograms next to report.json, gzip-compressed JSON lines; each line matches hist.v1.schema.json.

generator.description: The machine that generated load. Kept apart from the target: its CPU is not the target CPU.

cores.description: Logical CPUs visible to the tank process.

cpu_limit_cores.description: CPU quota of the tank container; null when unlimited.

source.description: cgroup_v1, cgroup_v2: the plugin reads the cgroup of the tank container itself (the ulta agent CPU reporter writes to its own upload queue, not to tank monitoring listeners). procfs: /proc/stat of the host. unavailable: nothing to read; saturation then relies on shots and plan.

util_pct_mean.description: Usage relative to cpu_limit_cores (or cores when unlimited).

throttled_periods_pct.description: Share of CFS periods in which the container was throttled.

throttled_s.description: Total time the container was throttled.

throttled_cores_mean.description: Mean throttled CPU time per second of the window, in cores: the quantity ulta reports as cpu_throttled_cores.

saturation.description: Whether the generator itself was the bottleneck. saturated when any signal crossed its threshold; unknown when the plugin had no data to judge.

value.description: The highest value over saturation.sustain_s seconds in a row of the window (the plugin section, 60 s by default; all of the window when shorter): for CPU_UTIL_HIGH the mean usage, for INSTANCES_EXHAUSTED the busy instances held all that time.

target.description: The service under load. The CPU model always names its source; Perforator data about the target is in perforator.json, not here.

cpu_model_source.description: perforator: Attributes.cpu of the target profiles, passed in the plugin section by the pre-shoot CI step (the plugin itself has no network).

cpu.description: Target CPU from a monitoring source; null when no source provides it. It is the CPU of the whole target, so the source delivers one series summed over pods (for Solomon: an expression that aggregates all series into one on the Solomon side, e.g. series_sum, with explicit metric_type and metric_name; any other Solomon sensor makes the source unsupported): the tank Solomon collector keeps one point per series name and second and would silently pass a single pod of several.

source_id.description: Id of the monitoring source the numbers come from.

cpu_ms_per_req.description: CPU milliseconds spent by the target per response: usage_cores_mean * 1000 / the mean rps of the window seconds up to the last usage point (monitoring points come late, and the seconds they have not reached would lower it on a rising load).

perforator.description: Perforator profiling of the target as known when the report is written. The plugin has no network access and writes pending (a microscope was passed in the plugin section) or not_requested; the terminal status is written by a CI step into perforator.json, which takes the actual shooting window from windows[id=test].

microscope_window.description: Window the microscope collects profiles in, as passed in the plugin section before the shooting; profiles exist only inside it.

process_comm.description: Target process name used to filter profiles (sidecars share the pod).

codes.description: Count per code; keys are decimal codes. net_codes counts every shot, including shots the generator discarded without sending (net code 777). http_codes and grpc_codes count sent requests by protocol code (0: no protocol response, e.g. a network error); discarded shots are not in them, nor in responses, rps, hist.v1 and cases.

latencyMs.description: Response time (interval_real) quantiles in milliseconds, computed by merging the per-second histograms of the window (hist.v1) by nearest rank. Shots the generator discarded without sending (net code 777; pandora writes them to phout with tag discarded and interval_real 0) are not in the histograms, so n is responses of the window, latency_overflow included. The rank of quantile p is k = ceil(p * n / 100), computed exactly (not in floating point); the value is the upper edge of the first grid bin where the cumulative count reaches k, converted to milliseconds: upper_us / 1000 (the 1000-1010 us bin gives 1.01). When k > n - latency_overflow the rank falls into the overflow and the value is null; so p100 is null whenever latency_overflow > 0, and latency_max_ms keeps the exact maximum. report.Validate checks the rank rule for every quantile. Reference for tests: numpy.percentile(interval_real, p, method='inverted_cdf') / 1000 over the raw values of the window without net code 777; the merged value is not below it and exceeds it by at most the width of the grid bin holding it, for any n. Keys are p1 to p99.999 (at most three decimals) and p100.

phase_index.description: Phase of a phase or steady window; the number in its id. A test window has none.

responses.description: Requests sent and completed in the window: sum(net_codes) - net_codes["777"]; report.Validate checks it. It is also n of the quantiles: discarded shots are not in the histograms.

rps_mean.description: responses divided by the window length in seconds.

latency_ms.description: null when the window has no responses.

latency_max_ms.description: Exact maximum of interval_real over the window, including responses beyond the histogram grid: the maximum of the per-second max that the tank aggregator computes from raw values. null when there are no responses.

latency_overflow.description: Responses longer than the last histogram grid edge (300 s): the sum of overflow over the hist.v1 lines of the window. They count in responses and in the quantile rank.

cases.description: Per-case (ammo tag) aggregates of the window. Discarded shots (net code 777, tag discarded in pandora) are not a case.

latency_max_ms.description: Exact maximum of interval_real over the window, including responses beyond the histogram grid: the maximum of the per-second max that the tank aggregator computes from raw values. null when there are no responses.

latency_overflow.description: Responses longer than the last histogram grid edge (300 s): the sum of overflow over the hist.v1 lines of the window. They count in responses and in the quantile rank.

rps.description: Requests sent and completed in this second: sum(net_codes) - net_codes["777"]; report.Validate checks it.

planned_rps.description: Planned rps of the second from the schedules, summed over pools; null when the plan of some pool is not in rps.

instances.description: Busy generator instances (pandora pool, phantom threads) from the aggregator stats; null when unknown: for a second without responses, and instead of 0, which pandora also reports when its expvar is unavailable.

required.description: The run is not suitable without this source; declared in the plugin section.

status.description: ok: data for the whole test window. partial: data with gaps; points missing only at the right edge of the test window, within the right-edge tolerance (plugin section, 60 s by default), are not a gap; points at or after the end of the test window are dropped. empty: no points came from the source (a Solomon token the server rejects looks the same: the tank Solomon plugin only logs the answer). error: the source failed, including a Solomon source without a token. pending: data may still arrive after the report was written; not allowed for a required source: the report is never changed, and the plugin does not wait in post_process, so a required source is reported by what arrived when the tank monitoring ended. unsupported: the source cannot be read in this setup, e.g. a Solomon sensor that may return several series. not_requested: listed but not collected in this run; not allowed for a required source.

profileString.description: String allowed in load_profile: letters, digits and _ . , : / ( ) + * - only. No JSON encoder escapes these characters, so the canonical JSON of load_profile is the same bytes in every language.

latencyOverflow.description: latency_overflow > 0: p100 is null and latency_max_ms is beyond the grid (over 300000 ms). Otherwise every quantile is a number and latency_max_ms is within the grid. A quantile other than p100 is null exactly when its rank is in the overflow, and latency_ms is null exactly when responses is 0; JSON Schema cannot compute the rank, report.Validate checks both.

targetCpuSeries.description: Target CPU point by point with the step of the source (15 s for Monium and Solomon), for the saturation point on line and step profiles, which have no steady windows. Written only when the plugin section sets target.cpu.series: true (off by default): without the option there is no series, and that is normal; with it the series is always here while target.cpu is not null. Points are usage_metric of the source target.cpu.source_id as the source delivered them, not resampled to seconds: target monitoring has no per-second precision. ts is cut to an integer second, of two points of one second the later stays; a negative usage is no CPU and no point. Only points with ts within the test window [start_ts, end_ts) are kept, as for the windows of target.cpu; the series is not split by window, a consumer finds the window of a point by its ts. At most one point per step_s seconds of the test window: a one-hour test gives 240 points with Monium (about 8 KB) and at most 3600 at a 1 s step (about 125 KB, less than load.per_second). Ascending ts with the smallest difference exactly step_s, points within the test window and ok without gaps between neighbours are checked by report.Validate.

status.description: ok: neighbouring points are exactly step_s apart and cover the test window: the first point at most two steps after start_ts, as for a monitoring source, and the last at most a step before the right-edge tolerance (plugin section, 60 s by default). Points missing within the tolerance with no point after them are late, not a gap; a point after them makes them a gap. partial: points with gaps. unavailable: no series although target.cpu is there, the cause is in reason, e.g. the step is unknown with fewer than two points in the test window.

step_s.description: Step of the source: the smallest difference of ts between neighbouring points; null when unavailable.

ts.description: ts of the point as the source gives it, cut to an integer second; for Solomon and Monium about the middle of its step.

cores.description: Target CPU usage at the point, in cores.
